questions.q: What is the Filesystem Hierarchy Standard (FHS)?
options: A security certification required to administer Linux servers
A Windows-only feature for assigning drive letters
The shared convention that defines what each top-level Linux directory (/etc, /var, /home, etc.) is for
A command used to format a new disk
questions.explain: The FHS is why / on nearly any Linux distro looks the same, letting you navigate an unfamiliar server because the layout is consistent.

questions.q: Where do system-wide configuration files live on a Linux system?
questions.explain: /etc is where nearly every service on the box reads its configuration settings from.

questions.q: Which directory holds data that changes while the system runs, like logs, mail queues, and caches?
questions.explain: /var stands for "variable" data — the opposite of the mostly-static installed software under /usr.

questions.q: A coworker says a service crashed overnight and asks you to find out why. Which directory should you check first?
questions.explain: /var/log/syslog (or /var/log/messages on RHEL-family systems) is the general system log and the first stop when troubleshooting an unexplained crash.

questions.q: What is the real difference between / and /root?
options: / is for temporary files and /root is for configuration files
/root is only used on Windows systems
/ is the top of the entire filesystem tree; /root is specifically the root user's home directory
They are two names for exactly the same directory
questions.explain: The root directory (/) is the single top of the whole tree, while /root is just one directory under it — the root user's personal home directory.
